item.title: Rain improves Dhaka’s air quality
item.description:
Dhaka's air quality was marked "moderate" Saturday morning due to rain in the capital city.
With an air quality index (AQI) score of 124 at 9:17am, Dhaka ranked 13th on the list of world cities with the worst air quality.
Pakistan’s Lahore, India’s Delhi and Afghanistan’s Kabul occupied the first three spots in the list, with AQI scores of 267, 133 and 195, respectively.
An AQI between 0 and 50 is considered to be "good" while between 50 and 100 it is considered "moderate", while an AQI between 101 and 200 is considered "unhealthy", particularly for sensitive groups.
Similarly, an AQI between 201 and 300 is said to be "poor'", while a reading of 301 to 400 is considered "hazardous", posing serious health risks to residents.
AQI, an index for reporting daily air quality, is used by government agencies to inform people how safe or polluted the air of a certain city is, and what associated health effects might be a concern for them.
In Bangladesh, the AQI is based on five criteria pollutants -- Particulate Matter (PM10 and PM2.5), NO2, CO, SO2 and Ozone.
Dhaka has long been grappling with air pollution issues. Its air quality usually turns unhealthy in winter and improves during the monsoon.
Air pollution consistently ranks among the top risk factors for death and disability worldwide.
As per the World Health Organization (WHO), air pollution kills an estimated seven million people worldwide every year, largely as a result of increased mortality from stroke, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer and acute respiratory infections.

item.title: The Rooppur reactor is ours. The fuel cycle isn't
item.description:
On Tuesday, November 17, 2026, at 3:16 PM, a controlled chain reaction on the bank of the Padma pushed 350 megawatts into the national grid.
Fifty years of waiting ended in a control room full of engineers who had probably stopped believing they would live to see it. Whatever else is true about Rooppur, that moment belongs to them, and to the country that paid for it.
What is happening to the bill for that moment is another matter.
The Tk26,181 crore increase in the project's cost is real, and it is almost entirely a currency story. The Russian credit was denominated in dollars at a projected Tk80; the rate is now Tk 122.40, and the taka lost more than 30% of its value after 2022.
Anyone presenting that arithmetic as a corruption story either cannot do the sum or is counting on you not doing it. The post-August 5 regime has been counting. 16 months into a mandate built on accountability, it has an Anti-Corruption Commission file alleging Tk590 billion in embezzlement, a figure repeated until it sounds like a finding, and no charge sheet a court has tested.
Rosatom denies the allegations and says procurement followed both countries' laws. Let that argument run its course. What cannot wait is the thing nobody is shouting about.
A reactor that runs is not a country that chooses. In October, five months after the first fuel assemblies went into the core, Dhaka signed a five-page memorandum with Washington on nuclear cooperation. It is non-binding. It creates no obligations. A document that obligates nobody is not a framework, it is a photograph of an intention.
Read it next to February's trade agreement and the picture sharpens. Bangladesh got its tariff cut, from 20% to 19%, worth roughly $85m a year on current export volumes. In exchange, the text commits Dhaka not to buy reactors, fuel rods, or enriched uranium from any country that jeopardizes essential US interests, with a narrow exception where an existing reactor has no alternative supplier. Article 4.3 lets Washington terminate the whole arrangement if Bangladesh enters a preferential trading relationship with a non-market economy.
Rooppur runs a Russian VVER-1200. Western reactors use different geometries and enrichment specifications, and conversion is economically prohibitive.
Every 12-18 months the core needs fresh fuel, and that fuel comes from Russia. The first reload falls due in 2027 or 2028. No clause in any of these documents hands Washington a veto tomorrow. What it hands Washington is a date, a supplier constraint, and a legal instrument, all timed to the moment our reactor becomes dependent and our leverage disappears. We did not sell a veto. We leased one.
The global order is fracturing, and middle powers are learning to work the fracture. The Hedgers , published by Cambridge in March, describes the method: Take what each power offers, concede in communiqués, never concede in contracts.
India is the model. It buys discounted Russian crude, keeps Russian spares flowing, deepens semiconductor and defense-technology ties with Washington, and gives ground in language it can withdraw later.
Bangladesh did the opposite, and did it in all three directions at once. Russian fuel, Chinese payment plumbing, American permission. We called it balancing. It was stacking: Three dependencies laid on top of each other until the whole structure rested on nothing that was ours.
Even the payment workaround is failing. CIPS was supposed to let us settle with Moscow in yuan. It has not. Banks in Dhaka and in China have both flinched at the sanctions exposure, instalments sit in a Sonali Bank account that cannot be moved, and Moscow now talks about rupees and a Russian bank branch in the capital. The plumbing exists on paper and jams in practice, which is what happens when you build a bypass out of other people's infrastructure.
Washington has done this before, and closer to home. In 1971 it sailed the USS Enterprise into the Bay of Bengal for no reason a Bangladeshi needs explained. Financial architecture is simply the quieter version of the same gesture.
None of this is a case for abandoning Rooppur, and it is certainly not a case for defaulting on the IMF. It is a case for spending the next 18 months differently.
Start with Moscow, where we have more leverage than we use. The delays hurt Rosatom too, and Russia has already waived penalties on the project and pushed the first principal repayment back to September 2028, which is not the behaviour of a creditor with no stake in keeping the reactor alive.
Dhaka should be asking now, formally and publicly, for a longer grace period and a restructuring of the repayment curve, and should ask as a partner with a working reactor rather than as a supplicant with a problem.
Then capture what the plant actually earns. Fully operational, Rooppur displaces billions of dollars of imported LNG and furnace oil every year. That is foreign exchange that currently vanishes into the fuel bill and will now stay home.
It should not be absorbed into general revenue and spent. It should be ring-fenced into a debt-servicing fund with statutory protection, so that the plant pays for itself and builds the buffer we will need the first time the taka slips again.
And diversify the balance sheet before the reload window closes. Bangladesh has been a shareholder in the New Development Bank since 2021 and has drawn on it; the bank is targeting $30bn of approvals across 2022 to 2026, with a rising share in local currencies.
Partner status in the BRICS architecture should be a standing diplomatic ask rather than an occasional communiqué line, and local-currency settlement with India and China should move from aspiration to agreement. India's caution about expansion is a real constraint. It is not a reason to stop asking.
This reactor will light homes for 60 years. We waited half a century for it, borrowed to build it, and are now being asked to trade the keys to its fuel cycle for a tariff cut that rounds to nothing.
The current is flowing. The country is not yet in the control room.
Zakir Kibria is a Bangladeshi writer, policy analyst, and entrepreneur based in Kathmandu, Nepal.

item.title: Justice for the Rohingya
item.description:
We are pleased to see that nearly a decade after Myanmar's brutal military crackdown in 2017, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) has delivered a landmark judgment, finding Myanmar responsible for committing genocide against the Rohingya community.
For the Rohingya, this has been a long and painful wait, and while it is undoubtedly a historic decision, it's also one that must lead to more than international condemnation.
The atrocities are not unknown: Thousands of Rohingya civilians were killed or subjected to widespread sexual violence and extreme brutality, and entire villages were destroyed.
These were not isolated incidents of violence. They were part of a systematic campaign against a vulnerable ethnic minority whose very existence was repeatedly denied.
For Bangladesh, this judgment carries particular significance. We have borne an enormous humanitarian and economic responsibility by sheltering more than a million Rohingya refugees for years despite stretched resources, yet the prospect of safe repatriation continues to look distant.
Bangladesh cannot be expected to shoulder this responsibility indefinitely while Myanmar evades accountability.
The ruling must now be followed by meaningful international action. The ICJ has called on Myanmar to facilitate the safe return of refugees and make reparations to victims. However, a court judgment alone cannot guarantee either.
The international community must now do its part to put pressure on Myanmar's military leadership, demand cooperation with investigations, and ensure that those responsible face consequences. Regional powers must also stop treating the crisis as a diplomatic inconvenience.
Repatriation must also be handled with care. Rohingya refugees cannot be sent back into the same conditions that forced them to flee. Their safety, citizenship rights, freedom of movement, and dignity must be guaranteed.
For too long, the Rohingya have been denied justice, identity and a place to call home. This judgment is an important step towards accountability; now the world must ensure it is not also the end of the effort.

item.title: UNICEF launches ‘Chain of Hope’ campaign for 60m children
item.description:
UNICEF on Thursday launched the Chain of Hope, a national campaign to turn political commitments into concrete action for Bangladesh's 60 million children, during a visit by Sanjay Wijesekera, the organization's regional director for Asia and the Pacific.
Launched on the eve of World Children's Day, the campaign is anchored in the Government of Bangladesh's Five-Year Strategic Framework for Reform and Development (July 2026–June 2031). It aims to translate national commitments into measurable results for children.
Building on the Child Rights Manifesto, endorsed by 12 political parties in December 2025, the campaign will mobilize parliamentarians, partners, communities, young people and the private sector around 5 priorities: advancing adolescent girls' rights, ending child labor, ensuring birth registration for every child, protecting children from climate change and tackling lead poisoning.
The campaign will advocate for policy reforms and stronger services, including closing legal loopholes that permit child marriage, integrating birth registration into public services to reach the 4 in 10 children under 5 whose births remain unregistered, making schools and health facilities more climate-resilient, and developing a strategy to end child labor.
Progress will be tracked against campaign milestones, with a report scheduled for publication by the end of December 2027.
The campaign's name draws on the image of Bangladesh's 60 million children holding hands to symbolically form a chain of hope around the world, united by their rights and aspirations.
“Every girl and every boy in Bangladesh deserves to grow up healthy, safe and protected, with the opportunity to learn and reach their full potential,” Wijesekera said.
“Yet too many children are still denied these rights. Through the Chain of Hope, we want to turn commitments into real changes in children's lives, backed by policies, resources and accountability. Because every child deserves more than promises. Every child deserves action.”
The urgency is reflected in the Bangladesh Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS 2025), which found that 47.2% of women aged 20–24 were married before the age of 18, while 9.2% of children aged 5–17 were involved in child labor.
The survey also found that only 59.2% of children under 5 had their births registered and that 38.4% of children aged 12–59 months had elevated blood lead levels.
During his 5-day visit to Bangladesh, Wijesekera met with Hafiz Uddin Ahmad, Speaker of the National Parliament; Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir, Adviser to the Prime Minister on Finance and Planning; and Salahuddin Noman Chowdhury, Foreign Secretary.
The meetings focused on national priorities for children and opportunities to translate commitments into action.
In Dhaka's Korail area, Wijesekera visited a UNICEF-supported Child Protection Community Hub, an Aalo Clinic and a wastewater treatment facility. He also met young peer leaders working to protect children in their communities.
He engaged with young climate activists, child journalists and members of UNICEF's Young People's Advisory Group, highlighting the importance of children's voices in decisions affecting their future.
In Cox's Bazar, Wijesekera visited learning, health and nutrition services in Rohingya refugee camps, witnessing how declining humanitarian funding threatens essential services for more than half a million children.
“Throughout my visit, from the communities of Dhaka to Cox's Bazar, I witnessed both the immense challenges children face and their extraordinary determination to build a better future,” Wijesekera said.
“Bangladesh's commitment to improving children's lives presents a critical opportunity for meaningful change.”

item.title: TBS NEWS AT 8 PM, 21 November 2026
ICBC 2026: Connecting academic knowledge with social realities, power and ethical responsibility
item.description:
The second chapter of the Multidisciplinary Biennial International Conference on ‘Bridging Cultures: Advanced Discourses (ICBC 2026)’ commenced its academic proceedings on Friday with an insightful online keynote address by Professor Azfar Hussain, a distinguished Bangladeshi-American theorist, literary critic, and interdisciplinary scholar affiliated with the Global Center for Advanced Studies (GCAS) and Grand Valley State University, USA.

Professor Hussain’s keynote address set an intellectually stimulating tone for the conference by critically examining contemporary academic discourses and the intersections of culture, literature, language, and knowledge production.

Drawing on his interdisciplinary scholarship, he highlighted the significance of critical inquiry in addressing the complexities of the contemporary world, encouraging participants to question established perspectives, interrogate dominant knowledge frameworks, and explore alternative possibilities for intellectual engagement.

His discussion further emphasised the importance of fostering dialogue across cultures and disciplines while connecting academic knowledge with social realities, power relations, ethical responsibility, and transformative intellectual practices.

In this regard, he said, “How do you do comparative literature? By making connections. But my argument has been, for quite some time, this that while making connections there are those who erase the actually existing unequal power relations on the one hand, and, on the other, also reinforce some kind of inequality.

“For instance, Nazrul; we tend to compare Nazrul to Byron and Shelly and Whitman. I understand, of course there are grounds for comparison but while comparing Nazrul to Shelly and Byron and the likes from Western canonical literature, there is also this tendency, a very implicit subtle tendency, to suggest that Nazrul’s greatness can be measured by the yardstick already set somewhere, by someone else or by some other power relations.

“I’m not against comparison; of course we have to compare but if you have to compare Kazi Nazrul Islam, why not compare him to a whole host of revolutionary poets that we have in Asia, Africa and Latin America…. making connections will be even more meaningful because, after all, Kazi Nazrul Islam is a revolutionary poet, he comes from a third world country, so let’s compare Kazi Nazrul Islam to other poets in Asia, African and Latin America.”

Speaking about the vision of ICBC 2026, Professor Dr Rahman M. Mahbub, Chair of the Conference, emphasised the importance of creating a shared intellectual space that transcends disciplinary and cultural boundaries and promotes inclusive, humane, and sustainable futures.

“One of the central objectives of ICBC is to bridge the boundaries that divide our knowledge, disciplines, cultures, and perspectives. We aspire to connect literature with philosophy, the humanities with the sciences, theory with practice, and technological innovation or AI with human values,” he said.

“I firmly believe that if science enables us to perform, create, and transform, the arts and humanities teach us to interpret, empathise, imagine, and understand the meaning of those achievements. The humanities give knowledge a human soul, while science expands the possibilities of human action. So, there should be a bridge between the soul and action – between Science and Humanities.  We need both as inseparable partners in advancing humanity,” Rahman M. Mahbub added.

Organised in a hybrid format, ICBC 2026 brings together an international community of scholars, researchers, academics, and students from diverse disciplinary backgrounds to foster intellectual exchange and interdisciplinary dialogue. The conference is jointly organised by City University, the Department of English Language and Literature, IBC Foundation, and IDEAS: International Journal of Literature, Arts, Science & Culture. 

The conference features eight distinguished keynote speakers, 15 plenary speakers, around 100 research paper presenters, and around 300 participants from Bangladesh and abroad. Its next sessions are scheduled for 22, and 23 November online at City University, followed by a full-day in-person programme at Bishwo Shahitto Kendro (BSK), Dhaka, on 26 November 2026.

Several eminent academicians joined the inaugural ceremony. The programme featured Brig Gen (retd.) Professor Dr Md Lutfor Rahman, Vice-Chancellor of City University, as the Chief Guest, while Professor Mashrur Shahid Hossain of Jahangirnagar University served as the Session Chair and Moderator.

The special guests included Professor Dr. Kazi Shahadat Kabir, Pro Vice-Chancellor of City University; Mahmudul Bari, Advisor, City University; and Professor Abu Zayed Mohammad, Dean, Faculty of Arts and Social Science, City University.

Their presence added significance to the occasion, reflecting the collective commitment of academic leadership and institutional collaboration towards advancing interdisciplinary scholarship and international academic engagement.

item.title: Former Awami League MPs' and mayor's homes attacked in Patuakhali
item.description:
The homes of three former MPs and a former municipal mayor belonging to the Awami League, whose activities are banned, were attacked and vandalised in Patuakhali.

The incidents took place between 10pm on Thursday and 9pm on Friday. Meanwhile, the homes of two leaders of the banned Chhatra League were also attacked and vandalised in Brahmanbaria.

On Friday evening, an anti-violence meeting was organised at the Kalapara upazila BNP office in Patuakhali.

Local MP and BNP central committee's training affairs secretary ABM Mosharraf Hossain addressed the meeting as the chief guest.

After the meeting, BNP leaders and activists held an anti-violence protest procession and rally in the upazila town.

Subsequently, the homes of two former MPs and a former municipal mayor came under attack and were vandalised.

The house of deceased former Awami League MP Anwar-ul Islam in the Kamarpatty area of Kalapara municipal town was attacked and vandalised around 7pm on Friday. He had served as an MP from 1991 to 1996 and died in 2024.

Later, around 8pm on Friday, a group of people threw brick chips and stones at the house of SM Rakibul Ahsan, former mayor of Kalapara Municipality and vice-president of the banned Awami League's upazila committee, in the Orphanage area.

About half an hour later, the residence of former state minister for disaster management and relief and former Patuakhali-4 MP Mohibbur Rahman was vandalised in Kalapara. He is a former vice-president of the Awami League's district committee.

Asked about the attacks and vandalism at the homes of two former MPs and a former mayor following the anti-violence meeting, Kalapara upazila BNP President Humayun Sikder told Prothom Alo, "Some Awami League activists have created an unstable situation. We held the anti-violence meeting in protest. The extent of the attacks and vandalism is not as has been portrayed. Perhaps the door was struck four or five times."

Kalapara Police Station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Md Nazrul Islam told Prothom Alo that they had received no complaints of such incidents.

Earlier, around 10pm on Thursday, the main gate of the house of former reserved-seat MP Lutfun Nessa in the Puran Bazar area of Patuakhali town was attacked and vandalised.

Her daughter-in-law, Roksana Parveen, said 30 to 35 people armed with locally made weapons broke the lock on the main gate of the boundary wall and attempted to enter the premises. Failing to get inside, they vandalised the main gate.

Lutfun Nessa served as a member of parliament from a reserved women's seat in the 10th parliament from 2014 to 2018. She is the wife of Sultan Ahmed, vice-president of the Awami League's Patuakhali district committee.

Patuakhali Sadar Police Station OC Md Moniruzzaman told Prothom Alo that police were sent to the former MP's residence after receiving information about the attack. Nobody filed a complaint at the time, and the police subsequently left.

Homes of two banned Chhatra League leaders attacked in Brahmanbaria

The homes of Mikail Hossain, joint secretary of the banned Chhatra League's district unit, and Sami Ahmed, president of its municipal unit, were attacked and vandalised in the Baganbari area of Brahmanbaria municipal town on Friday night.

The attackers smashed the Thai glass windows, chairs, tables and other furniture at the two houses.

Local residents said the homes of Mikail Hossain and Sami Ahmed were located in the Baganbari area of Brahmanbaria town. Nobody from Sami's family lives at his house.

Around 8pm on Friday, 15 to 20 young men wearing masks attacked the house. They initially hurled bricks and stones at it before smashing several windowpanes.

They then broke the lock of a food delivery office on the ground floor and vandalised its premises. Later that night, Mikail Hossain's house, which is also in the area, came under attack and was vandalised.

Sheikh Tanzim Hasan, a tenant at Sami Ahmed's house, said the attackers took away a motorcycle and a bicycle. However, none of the attackers could be identified because they were wearing masks.

A source said Mikail Hossain had recently engaged in a verbal altercation with a leader of Swechchhasebak Dal over comments on a Facebook post concerning a procession in the district town. The dispute reportedly led to the attacks.

Brahmanbaria district Chhatra Dal Member Secretary Samir Chakraborty said banned Chhatra League leaders Mikail Hossain and Sami Ahmed were attempting to create disorder, including through acts of sabotage, ahead of December. They had organised processions on several occasions.

"Ordinary people may have carried out these attacks out of anger over such activities," he said.

Brahmanbaria Sadar Police Station OC Khairul Alam said police were sent to the scene after receiving information about the incidents. They were investigating the identities of those involved.

item.title: Awami League’s dream of staging another 1/11 will turn into a nightmare: Hefazat-e-Islam
item.description:
Hefazat-e-Islam Bangladesh has said that the activities-banned Awami League’s dream of staging another 1/11 will be turned into a nightmare.

In a statement sent to the media today, Saturday, the party said the country’s sovereignty would remain unprotected unless Awami fascism was eradicated. It also said the Awami League must be banned as a political party through judicial proceedings at the tribunal for its responsibility for mass killings.

In the statement, Hefazat-e-Islam Ameer Allama Shah Muhibbullah Babunagari and Secretary General Allama Sajedur Rahman said, “We will turn their (the Awami League’s) dream of staging another 1/11 into a nightmare.”

BNP clashes with activities-banned Awami League in Pabna

The statement added, “We do not believe that the media outlets seen working in favour of their anti-Bangladesh agenda will be spared when another mass resistance takes place.”

The statement said the Awami League was no longer a political party. It said that, after carrying out mass killings in the face of the July mass uprising, the party’s leaders and activists had fled to India, proving themselves to be agents of hegemonic interests.

With support from Delhi, the defeated forces of 2024 were once again attempting to destabilise Bangladesh through acts of arson and violence across the country under Awami fascism, it added.

Why the government is not cracking down on Awami League sabotage yet, and its strategy

The top Hefazat leaders said in the statement that the victims killed and injured in the Pilkhana, Shapla, July and anti-Modi movements were still waiting for justice.

Public anger was growing towards those who spoke in favour of the Awami League and hegemonic interests on various talk shows and platforms without taking the victims’ demand for justice into consideration, they said.

The statement said the Awami League had been given opportunities to return to politics in the past as well. Even after coming to power in 1996 by seeking forgiveness through deception, the party had not reformed itself.

Constitution to be amended if necessary to permanently ban Awami League

Therefore, no one had the right to make any decision concerning the party that went against the aspirations of the families of those killed and the injured who had suffered under its brutal fascist rule in the previous Awami League regime, it said.

The Hefazat leaders said the Awami League could have no further political legitimacy in Bangladesh after seizing state power and carrying out enforced disappearances, killings and successive acts of genocide over 15 years, including at Pilkhana, Shapla and during the July uprising.

Unless Awami terrorism and fascism were eradicated, the country’s independence and sovereignty would remain unprotected, they said. Alongside united mass resistance, the Awami League must be banned as a political party through judicial proceedings at the tribunal for its responsibility for mass killings.

item.title: Admission to Class I: Lottery for Dhaka govt secondary schools on 15 Dec
item.description:
In the upcoming academic year (2027), students will be admitted to first grade through a lottery and from second to ninth grade through a written examination at 46 government secondary schools and three feeder branches in Dhaka Metropolitan.

The admission process will be conducted by dividing the schools into three groups.

For first-grade admission, a lottery will be held on 15 December.

The admission test for schools in Group ''A'' will be on 17 December, Group ''B'' on 18 December, and Group ''C'' on 19 December.

This information has been provided by the Directorate of Secondary and Higher Education. The admission test from the second to fifth grade will be out of 50 marks (15 in Bengali, 15 in English, and 20 in Mathematics), and from the sixth to ninth grade, it will be out of 100 marks (30 in Bengali, 30 in English, and 40 in Mathematics).

Quota allocation will be determined according to the policy for student admission to government secondary schools.
