item.title: Two Awami League leaders beaten up in separate Khulna incidents
item.description:
Two leaders of the activities-banned Awami League were beaten up and handed over to police by groups of people in separate incidents in Khulna on Saturday. Police said one of them was in critical condition.
The incidents took place at Sener Bazar in Rupsha upazila in the afternoon and near Fulbari Gate under Khan Jahan Ali Police Station in the evening.
The injured were identified as Md Moniruzzaman, also known as Monir Master, an Awami League leader and Laisuzzaman, 50, a member of the Muktijoddha Projonmo League. Laisuzzaman was reported to be in critical condition.
Moniruzzaman is the general secretary of the activities-banned Awami League's Ward No 5 unit in Deora under Aichgati Union. He is also the headteacher of Aichgati Belfulia Islamia High School and the younger brother of Professor Ashrafuzzaman Babul, former president of Khulna District Krishak League.
According to police and local sources, Laisuzzaman was beaten up over allegations that materials used to make crude bombs had been stored at the Muktijoddha Projonmo League office near Fulbari Gate. He was later taken to hospital in critical condition.
Police arrested a man named Miraj in connection with the incident.

item.title: Another 26 BGB platoons deployed in Gopalganj to maintain law and order
item.description:
An additional 26 platoons of Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) personnel have been deployed in Gopalganj to maintain law and order, bringing the total deployment in the district to 55 platoons.
The BGB headquarters confirmed the deployment in a press release issued on Saturday afternoon. According to the statement, the additional battalion has begun deploying alongside the 29 platoons already stationed in the district to maintain law and order, ensure public safety and prevent any untoward incidents.
According to the statement, an additional battalion comprising 26 platoons of BGB personnel has begun deploying alongside the 29 platoons already stationed in Gopalganj to maintain law and order, ensure public safety and respond to any untoward incidents.
The deployed personnel will work in coordination with the local administration and other law enforcement agencies to maintain normalcy.
They will also remain on high alert and perform their duties with professionalism and dedication to protect lives and property and maintain peace and order.

item.title: DU reopens Sheikh Mujibur Rahman Hall pocket gate after student protests
item.description:
The Dhaka University (DU) administration has reopened the pocket gate adjacent to Sheikh Mujibur Rahman Hall following protests by students demanding its removal from closure.
The gate was unlocked at 10:20pm on Saturday about half an hour after students launched a demonstration demanding its reopening.
Students initially gathered in front of Ziaur Rahman Hall around 9:50pm before marching to the pocket gate of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman Hall. They staged a protest there, joined by students from several other halls, including Ziaur Rahman Hall, Bijoy Ekattor Hall, Kabi Jasimuddin Hall and Surya Sen Hall.
DU Assistant Proctors Mir Muhammad Abdullah Al Mamun Ali and Professor Dr Enamul Haque Sajib were present at the scene. Students were also heard chanting “Bhua, Bhua” in their presence. The administration unlocked the gate around 30 minutes after the protest began.
The university administration had decided to temporarily close the pocket gate on November 17 at a coordination meeting, citing security concerns.
Since the closure, students had been demanding that the gate be reopened, saying it had caused inconvenience to their daily commute.

item.title: Police raid Gulshan house in search of ex-state minister Tarana Halim
item.description:
Police raided a house in Gulshan on Saturday in search of former Awami League lawmaker and state minister Tarana Halim, but did not find her there.
The raid was conducted at the house in Gulshan-2 on Saturday afternoon. Police remained at the premises until around 8pm, with 10 to 12 personnel and several detectives in plain clothes seen at the building.
Gulshan Police Station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Zayed Noor told Dhaka Tribune that police had visited the house based on specific information but did not find Tarana Halim there.
A security guard at the building, Sharif Mia, said police arrived shortly after 3pm. Some belongings were later brought downstairs from the flat, although Tarana Halim was not there.
“Madam is not at home. Her father lives on the fourth floor. Two female police officers went upstairs but did not bring anything out. No one was inside. The driver brought down some belongings,” he said.

item.title: Dhaka, Delhi to discuss water issues Sunday
item.description:
Bangladesh and India are set to hold a meeting under the Joint Rivers Commission (JRC) here on Sunday amid the urgency underscored by the Ganges Water Sharing Treaty, signed on December 12, 1996, which is due to expire on the same date this year.
The Indian delegation is already in Dhaka, and this will be the last meeting under the current treaty, a senior official told UNB on Saturday.
Md. Anwar Kadir, member, Joint Rivers Commission, Bangladesh, and Chairman, Joint Committee, Bangladesh side, will lead the six-member Bangladesh delegation at the meeting.
Sharad Chandra, Commissioner (FM) and Member, Joint Rivers Commission, India, will lead the Indian delegation.
Sanjay Kumar Gangwar, chief engineer, Central Water Commission; Ramesh Raj Sambharia, senior joint commissioner; Kanneluru Gautam, under secretary (IFD); Renjina Mary Varghese, under secretary (BM Division), Ministry of External Affairs, New Delhi; and Pooja Kumari Jha, second secretary (P&I), High Commission of India, are part of the Indian delegation.
Dr Md Sazzad Hossain, chief engineer, Hydrology, Bangladesh Water Development Board; Mohammad Abu Sayed, director, Joint Rivers Commission; Mohammad Samsuzzaman, Ministry of Water Resources; Md Baky Billah, director (South Asia-1), South Asia Wing, Ministry of Foreign Affairs; and Kazi Shahidur Rahman, executive engineer, Joint Rivers Commission, will join the meeting as members of the Bangladesh delegation.
Dhaka says it is a routine meeting, and the committee's responsibility is to ensure that the existing treaty is being implemented properly while treaty renewal or extension is not within the jurisdiction of this committee.
Official Spokesperson at the Ministry of External Affairs Randhir Jaiswal said the Joint Rivers Commission is the established mechanism to discuss all water-related, cross-boundary river-related issues, including the Ganga.
"The government of India remains committed to a constructive and forward-looking relationship with Bangladesh while safeguarding India's interest," he told reporters in New Delhi on Friday.
Securing its fair share of the transboundary rivers' waters is likely to become a major issue for Bangladesh in the coming days, making effective water diplomacy, international cooperation and constructive engagement with India increasingly important, officials and experts have said.
The government in Dhaka has been increasingly vocal in recent weeks, communicating a vision that Bangladesh will be seeking a new or revised agreement that safeguards its interests, particularly its share of dry-season flows, with the inclusion of a guarantee clause.
“Water could emerge as one of the major challenges for the entire world, including Bangladesh, in the future,” said Local Government, Rural Development and Co-operatives Minister Dr Abdul Moyeen Khan recently, stressing the need to integrate proper water management into national development planning.
Bangladesh and India share 54 transboundary rivers, but the Ganges remains the only one covered by a bilateral water-sharing agreement between the two countries.
Water Resources Minister Shahiduddin Chowdhury Anee said Bangladesh wants a new or revised Ganges agreement rather than simply renewing the existing treaty, with provisions guaranteeing its required share of water during the dry season.
“Our main priority will be to bring back the guarantee clause that was included in the 1977 agreement,” he said.
The 1977 agreement, negotiated by the BNP's founder Ziaur Rahman, included a safeguard stipulating that if the Ganges flow at Farakka fell below the level projected in the treaty to be provided to Bangladesh as its scheduled share during any 10-day period, the release to Bangladesh would not fall below 80% of that share.
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir recently said Bangladesh would seek an outcome that safeguards its national interests and security, including through a possible guarantee clause.
Asked whether the existing treaty would be renewed or replaced with a new agreement, he said, “Whatever is best for Bangladesh’s interest will be done.”
Foreign Minister Dr Khalilur, while attending the ninth Indian Ocean Conference in Mauritius, said they would like to see that there is an arrangement and a new treaty, or a revised treaty, ensuring the essential needs of their people.
“These are common rivers, and we have common legacies here, common interests, and, as I said, there's no other alternative but to seek a solution that is durable and will win public trust. And this will also be very important to lay the basis for the relationship over the next 25 to 50 years,” he told the media on the sidelines of the conference.
The foreign minister said they have done 55 years (of bilateral relations) already. “So, I don't think we should look at five years or ten years. We have to look at the very long term. So, mutual climate resilience as a priority in our foreign policies, our people policy, I should say, will actually be a key driver of the future.”

item.title: BNP procession attacked in Chittagong, 5 injured
item.description:
An attack was carried out by activists of the activities-banned Awami League on a procession organised by BNP leaders and activists in protest against terrorism and anarchy in Fatikchhari, Chittagong, on Saturday. Three motorcycles were set on fire and 15 others were vandalised in the incident. The BNP said 5 leaders and activists of the party and its affiliated organisations were injured.
The incident took place at around 5pm in the Shahi Mohammad Chowdhury Bari area of Kipaitennagar village in Nanupur Union of the upazila.
Local residents and police said a procession was brought out under the banners of Jubo League and Chhatra League at Nanupur Bazar in Fatikchhari upazila during Friday's Jumma prayers. The procession was led by local Jubo League leader Nurul Hakim.
In protest against the procession, BNP leaders and activists, along with members of its affiliated organisations, organised a counter-procession on Saturday afternoon. More than 100 leaders and activists took part in the procession on motorcycles.
When the procession reached the Kipaitennagar area, leaders and activists of the banned Chhatra League and Jubo League attacked them.
Two local residents who witnessed the incident said the Nanupur area is dominated by the Awami League. They said that when BNP activists set out in a procession that afternoon to catch Nurul Hakim, Jubo League and Chhatra League activists attacked them after announcing over a microphone that a robbery was taking place.
During the attack, 15 motorcycles were vandalised and 3 were set on fire.
Later, BNP activists returned with more party leaders and activists in a procession and vandalised Nurul Hakim's house. They also set fire to one motorcycle at the time.
On receiving the news, Fatikchhari Upazila Assistant Commissioner (Land) and Executive Magistrate Rahmat Ullah and police went to the scene.
Local BNP leaders said 5 BNP activists, including Akib, Robiul, Hossain, Manju and Yamin, were injured in the attack by Awami League activists. The injured were later given treatment locally. Among them, Hossain and Nazim were in serious condition.
Tension spread in the area following the incident.
Humayun Kabir, a leader of Nanupur Union BNP, told Dhaka Tribune: “In addition to campaigning on Facebook, Awami League activists attacked us after making announcements over loudspeakers. We were taking out a peaceful procession. But activists of the banned party had been lying in wait beforehand and carried out this attack. Five of our leaders and activists were injured. They also burnt three of our motorcycles and vandalised at least 15 motorcycles. Later, when we resisted, they fled.”
Fatikchhari Executive Magistrate Rahmat Ullah said: “The clash took place near Nanupur Bazar. After receiving the news, we went to the scene with the police but did not find anyone there. Two or three people were injured in the clash. They were taken to hospital. I have heard that several others were also injured. Besides, 10-12 motorcycles were vandalised and three were set on fire. Activists of the banned organisation carried out this attack on the Jubo Dal-Chhatra Dal procession after announcing over a loudspeaker that a robbery was taking place.”
Additional Superintendent of Police of Chittagong district (Hathazari Circle) Kazi Md Tarek Aziz told Dhaka Tribune: “After receiving news of the attack, a police team led by the Officer-in-Charge (OC) of Fatikchhari police station went to the scene. The situation is currently under control. Activists of the banned organisation carried out this attack.”
Fatikchhari police station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Robiul Alam Khan said: “After hearing about the attack, we went to the scene but did not find anyone. They had fled before that. Efforts are underway to identify and arrest them.”
Earlier, in Narail, leaders and activists of the BNP and its affiliated organisations brought out a procession on motorcycles on Wednesday afternoon (November 18) in protest against Awami League anarchy.
The procession passed through various roads in Kalia town. At around evening that day, while passing the boundary of the house of former member of parliament for Narail-1 constituency and Awami League leader Kabirul Haque Mukti and moving forward, activists of the Awami League and its affiliated organisations attacked them.
During the attack, Shaheen Molya, general secretary of Kalia Municipal Krishak Dal, and Sohel Molya, general secretary of the Kalia upazila unit of JASAS, were hacked and injured. They died while being taken to Khulna.

item.title: 'I'll be back': vows Kane after ankle surgery
item.description:
Bayern Munich's star striker Harry Kane pledged to return for the "business end of the season" after undergoing surgery on his left ankle on Saturday.
Kane limped off after 20 minutes of Bayern's 1-1 home draw with Cologne in their Bundesliga match on Friday, the club confirming the England captain had torn a ligament in his ankle.
Bayern issued a statement Saturday saying the Ballon d'Or winner had "successfully undergone surgery" on his left ankle.
"The 33-year-old will now begin his rehabilitation program," Bayern said, with the injury expected to keep Kane out for three to four months.
Kane posted a picture on social media from his hospital bed on Saturday, vowing to work his way back to fitness this season.
"The highs and lows of life! Obviously very disappointed to get this injury but as always it's an opportunity to show resilience and improvement going into 2027.
"I'll be back fresh and ready to go for the business end of the season."
Kane shared a quote from three-time Super Bowl-winning wide receiver Julian Edelman: "tough times don't last, tough people do", while thanking his supporters for their messages of support.
Kane has a history of ankle issues although he has only missed a handful of games since moving to Bayern in 2023.
England coach Thomas Tuchel will be keeping a keen eye out on how England's most capped player's rehabilitation progresses.
England play Norway in the Nations League quarter-finals in late March.
The injury comes at a difficult time for Bayern, who are currently missing several players, particularly up front.
Bayern are without Luis Diaz, Serge Gnabry, Alphonso Davies, Ismael Saibari and captain Manuel Neuer, while midfielder Jamal Musiala and coach Vincent Kompany both returned after long lay-offs on Friday.

item.title: Mushfiqur ruled out of 2nd SA Test with groin injury
item.description:
Bangladesh veteran batter Mushfiqur Rahim was ruled out of the second Test against South Africa after sustaining a groin injury. The last and final Test starts at Centurion on Monday as Bangladesh will be looking to level the series following a nine-wicket defeat in the opening Test.
"Mushfiqur complained of acute pain in the left groin region during the first Test match. Following the Test, he underwent an MRI scan and the results confirmed some inflammation and irritation around the bony pelvis," National team Physio Bayjedul Islam Khan said.
"He requires immediate rest and targeted rehabilitation to manage the stress response and prevent further aggravation and is unavailable for the second Test," the national team physio said.
Mushfiqur made 0 and 22 in the first Test and scored just one fifty in his last 10 innings.

item.title: What are we failing to teach?
item.description:
“He who studies rides in cars and carriages.”
This familiar Bengali proverb is something many of us grew up hearing. It reflects a traditional understanding of education: S tudy hard, achieve good results, secure a good job, and build a prosperous life.
There is nothing wrong with that aspiration. Education should certainly provide children with the knowledge and skills they need to earn a living and improve their financial and material well-being.
But is that all education is meant to achieve?
Nearly 30 years ago, Une sco ’s Delors Report (1996) identified four broad purposes of education: “ L earning to know,” “learning to do,” “learning to be,” and “learning to live together.”
The first two concern knowledge and skills, while the latter two focus on developing the whole person and preparing young people for life with others.
In our education system, academic knowledge and examination performance naturally receive considerable attention. Yet in practice, “learning to be” and “learning to live together” often receive far less attention than academic achievement and job-related skills.
Are we educating students merely to pass examinations and acquire subject knowledge, or are we also helping them become confident, resilient, and emotionally healthy individuals who can understand others, navigate differences, build meaningful relationships and live well together?
Beyond the marks and grades
“Learning to be” is about becoming a complete human being, not simply a successful student. Education should help young people think independently, ask questions, communicate clearly, make thoughtful decisions, and reflect on their actions.
It should also nurture emotional intelligence, so they can understand their emotions, recognize different perspectives, respond with empathy, and build healthy relationships. Along the way, they need to develop confidence, resilience, integrity, and a sense of responsibility.
Yet these qualities can easily be overshadowed when educational success is measured mainly through marks, grades, examination results, and admission to prestigious institutions. Curiosity, creativity, empathy, and resilience may become secondary to the next examination or academic milestone.
Academic excellence matters. The concern arises when academic achievement becomes almost the sole measure of success. A student may achieve excellent grades and build a successful career while still struggling to handle failure, accept criticism and different opinions, acknowledge mistakes or work with people who are different.
That takes us to a deeper purpose of education. Beyond what students know and what they achieve, what kind of human beings are they becoming?
The answer cannot come only from what is prescribed in the curriculum or written in textbooks. It also depends on how children experience and engage with the world around them, how they interact with others, respond to differences, handle disagreements, and take responsibility for their actions. That is where “learning to live together” becomes equally important.
A child walks into a classroom carrying much more than a schoolbag. He or she carries a family background, social, and religious identity, hopes, fears, abilities, opportunities, and disadvantages. Yet once inside the classroom, all children are expected to learn together. The deeper question is whether we are also helping them learn how to live together.
This matters deeply in a socially diverse and economically unequal society such as Bangladesh. Children grow up with different levels of wealth, different beliefs, abilities, languages, family circumstances, and social experiences.
From an early age, they begin to notice who is respected, who is ignored, who is included, and who is left out. In this way, they begin to form ideas about fairness, often without being explicitly taught.
Discrimination does not always appear as open exclusion. It can take the form of a joke, a stereotype, a label, an unequal expectation or an assumption about what a child can achieve.
A child from a poorer family may be made to feel inferior. A child with a disability may be viewed as incapable rather than supported to participate. A child who is different from the majority may gradually feel that belonging is something to be earned rather than something everyone deserves.
Schools can either reinforce these attitudes or challenge them. A school that teaches equality but allows a child to be humiliated because of family circumstances sends a contradictory message. A school that speaks about inclusion but does not enable a child with a disability to participate fully does the same. Similarly, when academic competition dominates school life, children may learn to see one another more as rivals than as people with whom they can learn and grow.
This is why values cannot be taught only through lessons, definitions, or moral instruction. Children learn from what they experience.
A child who is listened to learns that his or her voice matters. A child who is treated with dignity learns what dignity means. A child who is allowed to make a mistake without humiliation learns that failure is part of learning. A child who sees others treated fairly begins to understand fairness not as an abstract principle, but as something that should guide everyday life.
The same is true of disagreement. Children will argue, compete, form friendships, and sometimes hurt one another. School can teach them that disagreement does not have to lead to hostility. Learning to live together does not mean teaching children to agree on everything. It means helping them learn how to disagree without hatred, humiliation, or exclusion.
Cooperation also has to be experienced, not simply encouraged. When children work together on projects, solve problems collectively, or take responsibility for shared activities, they learn to listen to different opinions, share responsibilities, and recognize the contribution of others. These are not activities outside education. They are part of what education should accomplish.
The purpose is not to make children identical in their beliefs, abilities or experiences. It is to help them understand that difference does not have to become division. In a diverse society, children need to learn how to live with people who may think differently, believe differently, or come from circumstances very different from their own.
Learning to live with nature
“Learning to live together” should extend beyond human relationships to our relationship with nature. Children need to experience that they are not separate from the natural world, but part of it, and that nature is not merely a resource for human use. It has its own value and deserves care and respect.
This understanding cannot come from textbooks alone. Children need opportunities to experience nature, observe living things, grow plants, understand water and waste, and see how human actions affect the world around them.
The aim is not simply to teach children about the environment, but to help them develop a sense of belonging to nature and responsibility towards it. To live well is not only to live well with one another, but to live with nature in a way that respects its right to exist and flourish.
Education for life
Education should prepare children not only for work, but for life; not only to compete, but to cooperate; and not only to succeed as individuals, but to live together as human beings.
Its real measure lies not only in what children know or achieve, but in who they become and how they treat others. Can they live meaningful lives, respect differences, respond to inequality, participate responsibly in society, and care for the world they share?
The question before us, therefore, is not simply what technical skills our children acquire, but what kind of people our education institutions are helping them become.
And ultimately, what kind of society will those people build?
Dr Somnath Saha is Assistant Professor, Brac IED, Brac University.

item.title: The government gets something right
item.description:
It's easy enough -- and I do it often enough -- to point to something a government is doing wrong and then snarl about that thing the government is doing wrong. It is more difficult to find something a government is doing right and then congratulate that government.
It's possible to go on and say that this is because governments do so many things wrong and so few right -- but that would be cynical. I am indeed cynical, but at least part of this is that it's so much more fun to criticize than it is to praise.
Yet here we are, the Bangladeshi government is getting a good part of cleaning up the banking system right.
We all wish we weren't here in the first place of course. We'd all prefer that there weren't years and years where well connected people were able to pillage the banking system. Yet there were, and we've now got to deal with what did indeed happen.
What happened is that people borrowed money they had little ability to repay -- or little intention to repay. That causes a significant problem for the rest of us because stealing from banks is not victimless.
Too many loans not repaid means the bank will -- eventually -- run out of capital and fail.
If the banks fall over, then a basic requirement for a useful economy stops happening -- our savings stop being recycled into the investments that make the future richer. We do not want this to happen.
One part of this is to identify and isolate those banks that have lost some or all of their capital. This is being done : “15 banks, including five merged Shariah-based banks, were behind more than 85% of the over Tk600,000 crore in non-performing loans (NPLs).”
Some of the NPLs are just loans that didn't work. That always does happen and a system that had none at all would be a system that wasn't lending enough money -- thereby failing to make the future richer. But a large portion of these were loans that should never have been made -- to those who could not, or would not, repay them. People who were insiders at the banks and were able to short-circuit the normal lending standards.
So, now we know which banks have these problems. We can then use special measures to manage these banks. Insist that they raise more capital. Merge some of them. Keep a special eye on who they lend to. If necessary -- and we don't like doing this but sometimes we must -- put more tax money into the banks so they have capital again.
We also want to punish those who borrowed and did not repay. This is also being done : “A court in Chittagong on Thursday sentenced former land minister Saifuzzaman Chowdhury Javed to 15 years in prison for embezzling Tk25 crore in loans from United Commercial Bank Limited (UCBL) and laundering the money abroad.”
This is also good and the right thing to do. Thieves should go to jail and thieves who threaten the entire economic system with their thefts should spend more time in jail than those who steal lesser things.
We're never going to catch everyone who stole from the banks. But that's not actually the point. While it would be nice to punish them it's still not the point. It would be just to jail them all, but even that's not the point.
What we must do is make sure that no one steals from the banking system in the same way again. Because, as above, having a banking system is what makes the joint future richer. So we need to protect the banking system itself, not just some of the money in some of the banks.
Fifteen years -- plus a fine -- is a hefty sentence. The next man who decides he'd like to defraud a bank will think quite a lot about whether he's willing to risk it. Sure, it's great to fine as well and that might put some of the money stolen back into the bank.
The correct reaction to a banking system that has been pillaged is for the central bank -- and so the taxpayers -- to recapitalize the banks so that there is still a functional banking system.
This is needed to make the future richer. Then we need to visit those who stole all the money with prosecutions and long jail sentences so that no one tries this again.
The Bangladesh Bank, the government, is starting to do this. Good. We can be cynical and think that most governments don't do many good things. But that just makes praising the few done even more important. So, well done.
Tim Worstall is a senior fellow at the Adam Smith Institute in London.

item.title: Restoring calm to the nation
item.description:
The latest wave of arson, crude-bomb explosions, attacks on homes and public institutions, and road blockades across the country is terrorizing the nation, and as such, has veered away from mere political conflict into a direct assault on public safety, livelihoods, and the right of ordinary citizens to go about their lives without fear.
Such violence must be condemned unequivocally.
The incidents reported are alarming in both their scale and targets: Police stations torched, ancestral and present homes and businesses vandalized; vehicles set ablaze. These actions have resulted in the loss of lives, and if this is not senseless violence, then nothing is. These are not isolated incidents that can be brushed aside as routine political tension. They point to a dangerous erosion of public order that demands an immediate and decisive response.
There can simply be no justification for setting fire to buildings, hurling crude bombs, attacking police personnel, or targeting homes and businesses over their owners' political affiliations.
There should not be a need for editorials in newspapers to understand that political parties and their supporters should be refraining from using street violence and disruption as a shortcut to force political comebacks. It goes without saying that this is neither legitimate politics nor what ordinary citizens expect from those seeking public trust. Grievances must be pursued through peaceful channels, and those who organize, finance, or carry out attacks must be prosecuted, regardless of their political connections.
At the same time, resolving deep political friction requires genuine engagement: To that end, the government must consider keeping the door open to political dialogue. Having said that, it must, without fail, ensure that it never projects weakness or cedes the initiative to anarchic elements. This lax treatment of such incidents is partially the reason why mob violence has grown so rampant over the past couple of years.
Restoring order also requires empowering law enforcement agencies with a clear, unambiguous mandate to enforce the law and protect public life and national assets. When police stations, transport corridors, and private properties are repeatedly targeted across districts, reactive measures are no longer tenable. Intelligence gathering, preventive policing, and rapid intervention must be strengthened so citizens see an effective security strategy and can begin to feel more secure.
Firm enforcement must also remain rooted in the rule of law. A security crackdown cannot become a licence for arbitrary arrests or political profiling, something that we have also regrettably seen too much of in recent times.
Detaining individuals without credible evidence of specific offenses only deepens public mistrust and fuels instability. Arrests must be evidence-based, detainees' rights respected, and investigations conducted transparently and impartially so that every citizen - regardless of political affiliation - is assured equal protection.
People should not have to weigh the risk of a bomb blast or a burning vehicle before sending their children to school, commuting to work, or moving freely around their cities. If there is to be peace in the nation, the government must demonstrate both political maturity and state resolve: Meaningful dialogue paired with decisive, lawful policing, clear accountability, and a zero-tolerance stance toward political violence.
Our nation cannot and must not be left at the mercy of those looking to destabilize it.

item.title: Greek PM under fire over Grand Theft Auto post
item.description:
Greece’s prime minister has come under fire for asking youngsters whether they’d like the mature-content Grand Theft Auto VI videogame for Christmas.
“Which of you will ask for Grand Theft Auto VI as a Christmas present from grandad and grandma?” Kyriakos Mitsotakis said in a TikTok post on Friday, with the game’s logo briefly flashing on-screen.
“We all know that grandfathers and grandmothers rarely say no to their grandchildren,” he added.
The post was designed to promote a 400-euro pension bonus from Mitsotakis’ government, as it faces elections next year.
But it came under attack from critics calling it inappropriate to encourage minors to buy a mature game.
“The prime minister ‘promotes’ a video game that is banned for minors just to follow the trend,” the main opposition socialist Pasok party said.
Leftist daily Efsyn called the move a “gaffe” while conservative newspaper Dimokratia said it was a “tragic” error.
Ironically, Mitsotakis’ government has joined a growing number of countries imposing curbs on young people’s use of social media.
Like its predecessors, GTA VI is an open-world action game in which players roam freely through a sprawling city, stealing cars, pulling off heists and carrying out missions for criminal gangs.
Containing intense violence, gore, sexual content, nudity, strong language and drug and alcohol use, it has an age rating of 17 or above.
Coming after a 13-year hiatus in the series, the game has been a smash hit worldwide, raking $3.79 billion in retail sales on its first day according to its publisher Rockstar Games.

item.title: BRAC NextGen showcases talents of 2,000 students in Savar
item.description:
BRAC NextGen 2026 held its central final showcase at BRAC CDM in Savar on Saturday, bringing together around 2,000 students from BRAC Secondary Schools to celebrate their talents in dance, music, visual arts and social innovation.
The initiative aims to identify and nurture students' talents beyond conventional academic learning while developing their creativity, confidence, communication, leadership and problem-solving skills.
The programme featured four competition categories: MOVE for dance, VOICE for singing, CANVAS for drawing and visual arts, and SOLVE for social innovation.
Students presented dance and musical performances, displayed their artwork and proposed solutions to problems affecting their schools, families and communities.
The 58 finalists were selected following school-level competitions and evaluations of artistic submissions, recorded performances and innovative ideas. They subsequently attended a three-day mentoring bootcamp, where experts provided guidance and practical training to help them develop their skills and presentations.
Through SOLVE, students identified local challenges and proposed practical solutions. CANVAS provided a platform for artistic expressions of their experiences, dreams and aspirations, while MOVE and VOICE highlighted their performing arts talents.
The cultural performances included classical dance, Nazrul Nritya and a musical drama based on Rabindranath Tagore's Chitrangada.
BRAC Executive Director Asif Saleh attended the event as chief guest.
Other guests included Aarong Chief Business Officer Tanvir Hossain, BRAC Chief People and Culture Officer Moutushi Kabir, BRAC Senior Director for Education, Skills Development and Migration Safi Rahman Khan, and BRAC Education Programme's Head of Social Enterprise Niveen Reza.
Addressing the event, Asif Saleh said the students' artwork, performances and innovative ideas demonstrated their ability to think creatively.
He said the initiative aimed to provide a platform where students could develop their perspectives, explore their interests and realise their potential.
Moutushi Kabir said the students' creativity and innovative thinking offered hope for the country's future, adding that they had the potential to contribute to positive change in Bangladesh.
Safi Rahman Khan said BRAC hoped participants would share their experiences and learning with students at their respective schools.
He also expressed the ambition to expand the initiative next year, allowing more students from BRAC's 12 secondary schools to participate and potentially extending the platform to other students across the country.
Niveen Reza said the initiative was designed to identify and nurture students' talents through mentorship while creating opportunities for them to connect, showcase their work and learn from one another.
BRAC plans to develop the initiative beyond an annual competition through a proposed BRAC NextGen Fellows programme, which would provide selected students with continued mentorship, skills development and opportunities to participate in national competitions and exhibitions.
The organisation is also exploring ways to support promising SOLVE projects through pilot testing and practical implementation.
The initiative further aims to encourage participants to share their skills and experiences with peers, helping promote creativity and innovation across BRAC Secondary Schools.

item.title: Green University hosts Career Expo 2026
item.description:
Green University of Bangladesh (GUB) organized Career Expo 2026 at its permanent campus in Purbachal American City on Saturday, bringing together 68 companies and industry representatives to connect students with potential employers.
The event was organized by the university's Centre for Career Development (CCD).
GUB Vice-Chancellor Professor Mohammad Shorif Uddin attended the inauguration as the chief guest, while Pro-Vice-Chancellor Professor Khawza Iftekhar Uddin Ahmed attended as the special guest. CCD Director Serajum Munira delivered the welcome address.
Representatives from various sectors, including human resource professionals, corporate executives, teachers, university officials, students and young professionals, participated in the day-long event.
The expo featured 5 panel discussions and 2 roundtable sessions, with 48 senior executives and industry leaders, including human resource specialists from various organizations, taking part.
The discussions focused on the future workforce, employment-oriented skills, talent management, technology-driven human resource management, leadership development, workplace transformation in the age of artificial intelligence (AI), and industry-academia collaboration.
Speaking at the event, Vice-Chancellor Mohammad Shorif Uddin said direct interaction with corporate leaders and potential employers would help students understand the practical demands of the workplace.
He said the expo would provide students with practical insights and guidance to prepare for employment opportunities at different companies.
He added that such events would help students develop professional skills, communication abilities and leadership qualities while adapting to changes in the industry.
Pro-Vice-Chancellor Khawza Iftekhar Uddin Ahmed said the university was organizing the career expo for the second time following the success of its previous edition.
He said the event would give students an opportunity to strengthen their skills and prepare for entering the job market.
The expo brought together companies and organizations from a wide range of sectors, including aviation, manufacturing, information technology, recruitment, financial services, education, retail, hospitality, food and beverage, and renewable energy.
Participating organizations included US-Bangla Airlines, Crown Cement, Transcom Electronics, Genex Infosys, Jibon Bima Corporation, BRAC Institute of Skills Development, ACI Logistics (Shwapno), Apex Footwear, Kazi and Kazi Tea Estate, and Greenery Energy Solutions, among others.Limited, while Greenery Energy Solutions Limited represented the renewable energy sector.

item.title: 87 crude bomb explosions, 83 vehicles set on fire in 13 days
item.description:
Police recorded 87 crude bomb explosions at different locations and 83 incidents of vehicle arson across the country in 13 days, from November 7 to 19.
The information was provided by the Police Headquarters on Saturday.
During the period, police installations and vehicles also came under attack. A total of 39 cases have been filed over the incidents, and 66 people have so far been arrested, according to the Police Headquarters.
According to police data, 4 police installations were subjected to arson and vandalism, while 28 vehicles were also targeted in arson and vandalism across the country.
In addition, 3 installations and 1 vehicle were damaged in crude bomb explosions.
Police Headquarters Assistant Inspector General (Media and Public Relations) Kamarum Munira said various measures were underway to maintain normal law and order.
These include collecting advance intelligence, increasing police surveillance and patrols, setting up checkpoints, and responding as quickly as possible.
She said police were performing their duties with the highest level of vigilance to prevent banned organizations and parties whose activities are prohibited from attempting any form of sabotage.
She also warned that any attempt to carry out sabotage would be dealt with strictly.

item.title: Land minister assures land and financial support for IDEB’s development
item.description:
Land Minister Mizanur Rahman Minu has assured cooperation for the development of diploma engineers, enhancement of their professional dignity, and expansion of institutional infrastructure.
He gave the assurance while speaking as the chief guest at a discussion meeting held at the Institution of Diploma Engineers, Bangladesh (IDEB) auditorium in Rajshahi on Saturday, marking IDEB's 56th founding anniversary and Mass Engineering Day-2026
The land minister said the contribution of diploma engineers is extremely important for the development and progress of the country. “Behind the development of developed countries in the modern world, there is an important role of skilled engineers.”
He said diploma engineers are working tirelessly for the infrastructure development, industrialization and technical advancement of Bangladesh. Equal participation of both men and women must be ensured in the development of the country, he added.
“It is especially necessary to increase opportunities for women in technical education and employment. If women can be made economically self-reliant, the overall economy of the country will become stronger.”
The minister also said emphasis should be given on improving the quality of technical education and modern training to increase the professional skills of diploma engineers and their job opportunities in the international labor market.
Regarding the infrastructural limitations of IDEB, he said, there is a need for sufficient space to expand the activities of the institution. Initiatives will be taken to find possible land in this regard. He also assured financial support from the Ministry of Land.
The chief discussant at the event was Engineer Kabir Hossain, Convener of the Interim Central Committee of IDEB. The event was presided over by Engineer Md. A. R. Jamil Idir, Convener of the District Executive Committee of IDEB.
